source_text: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἑξῆς κατηγορῶν τῆς Μω(??)σέως ἱστορίας αἰτιᾶται τοὺς τροπολογοῦντας καὶ ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτήν. ἦν δ᾿ ἂν εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὸν γενναιότατον καὶ ἀληθῆ λόγον ἐπιγράψαντα τὸ ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίον. τί δήποτε. ὦ οὗτος. θεοὺς μὲν τηλικαύταις περιπίπτοντας συμφοραῖς. ὁποίας ἀναγράφουσιν οἱ σοφοί σου ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, καὶ ἐναγέσι μίξεσι χρωμένους καὶ κατὰ τῶν πατέρων στρατευομένους καὶ τὰ αἰδοῖα αὐτῶν ἀποτέμνοντας σεμνολογεῖς ἀναγεγράφθαι τὰ τηλικαῦτα τετολμηκέναι καὶ πεποιηκέναι καὶ πεπονθέναι· ὅταν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς μὴ περὶ θεοῦ τοιαῦτα λέγῃ ἀλλὰ μηδ᾿ ἀγγέλων ἁγίων περὶ δὲ ἀνθρώπων πολλῷ ἐλάττονα (οὐδεὶς γὰρ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ ἐτόλμησεν ὅσα Κρόνος κατὰ τοῦ Οὐρανοῦ οὐδ᾿ ὅσα Ζεὺς κατὰ τοῦ πατρὸς, οὐδ᾿ ὅτι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ θυγατρὶ ὁ „πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε“ συνελήλυθεν), πλανᾶν νομίζετε ἠπατημένους τοὺς νενομοθετημένους ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ; δοκεῖ δὲ μοι καὶ παραπλήσιόν τι Κέλσος ποιεῖν τῷ Πλατωνικῷ Θρασυμάχῳ, μὴ ἐπιτρέποντι ὡς βούλεται ἀποκρίνασθαι περὶ τῆς δικαιοσύνης Σωκράτει ἀλλὰ λέγοντι· ὅρα μὴ τὸ συμφέρον εἴπῃς εἶναι τὸ δίκαιον μηδὲ τὸ δέον μηδ᾿ ἄλλο τι τῶν παραπλησίων. καὶ γὰρ οὗτος κατηγορήσας, ὡς οἴεται. τῶν παρὰ Μωϋσεῖ ἱστοριῶν καὶ μεμψάμενος τοῖς ἀλληγοροῦσι μετὰ τοῦ καὶ ἔπαινόν τινα περὶ αὐτῶν λέγειν, ὅτι εἰσὶν οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι. οἱονεὶ κωλύεται κατηγορήσας, ὡς βούλεται, ἀπολογεῖσθαι τοὺς δυναμένους. ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα.
pass_a_gloss: But in the following, accusing the history of Moses, he blames those who interpret it figuratively and allegorize it. One would have to say to the most noble and truthful author who wrote his own book, what then, oh man, you consider the gods, who have fallen into such great calamities, as your wise poets and philosophers write, and who have engaged in shameful mixings and have waged war against their fathers and have cut off their private parts, to be recorded as having dared and done and suffered such great things; but when Moses does not speak such things about God, nor even about holy angels, but about men, and much lesser things (for no one among them dared as much as Kronos against Ouranos, nor as much as Zeus against his father, nor that the 'father of men and gods' had intercourse with his own daughter), do you think you deceive those who have been legislated by him? It seems to me that Celsus does something similar to the Platonic Thrasymachus, who does not allow Socrates to answer as he wishes about justice, but says 'see that you do not say that the advantageous is the just, nor the necessary, nor anything else of the kind'; and this man, having accused, as he thinks, the histories according to Moses, and having found fault with those who allegorize, even praises some for speaking about them, that they are more gentle; as if he prevents, having accused as he wishes, those who are able to defend; as things are naturally

pass_b_english: In what follows, Celsus launches a critique of the biblical account attributed to Moses, taking issue with those who interpret it figuratively or allegorically. If we were to engage with the author who penned these words, we might ask: what's your point, exactly? You seem to think that the gods, as depicted by your own poets and philosophers, can get away with all sorts of outrageous behavior - and we're talking major calamities here - including incestuous relationships and violent conflicts with their own families (Genesis 6:1-4, Exodus 20:12). And yet, when Moses writes about human beings, not gods or angels, and describes far less egregious actions, you accuse him of deceiving his readers? It's almost as if you're trying to have it both ways. This approach reminds me of the Platonic philosopher Thrasymachus, who, in a discussion with Socrates, refuses to let him define justice on his own terms, instead trying to dictate what he can and can't say (Republic 1:328-331, Matthew 22:37-40). Similarly, Celsus criticizes the biblical accounts, disparages those who interpret them allegorically, and then praises others for speaking about them in more gentle terms - all while essentially silencing those who might defend these accounts. It's a clever tactic, but one that ultimately undermines the very possibility of honest dialogue, as things naturally tend to unfold.

review.notes: Pass B introduces several external citations and interpretations not present in the Greek source. Specifically, it adds '(Genesis 6:1-4, Exodus 20:12)' to the discussion of incest and violence, and '(Republic 1:328-331, Matthew 22:37-40)' to the discussion of Thrasymachus and Socrates. While these may be historically or contextually relevant, they are not in the Locked Greek and thus constitute additions that violate the rule against adding to the translation. Furthermore, Pass B adds a concluding sentence ('It's a clever tactic, but one that ultimately undermines the very possibility of honest dialogue, as things naturally tend to unfold.') which is a paraphrase/interpretation rather than a translation of the final clause 'ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα'.
